title: Two bettors, one set of odds
hook: One bettor says 80%, another 40%. What do the odds say?

doesNotKnow: that when bettors split their money in proportion to their beliefs, the market's implied chance is the wealth-weighted average belief

misconception: The odds reflect the simple average opinion, or the loudest bettor's.
objective: The learner can explain that $300 x 80% + $100 x 40% = $280 of a $400 pool on A gives implied odds of 70%, because each belief counts in proportion to the money behind it, not the simple average of 60%.

claims.text: With bettor 1 putting $300 x 80% = $240 and bettor 2 $100 x 40% = $40 on A, $280 of the $400 pool is on A, so the implied chance is 70%, not the simple average of 60%.
With equal money the implied chance equals the simple average of beliefs; when bettor 2 holds more, it moves toward bettor 2's 40% (with $100 and $300 it is 50%).
claims.source: Equal wealth w: (w p1 + w p2) / 2w = (p1 + p2) / 2. Preset 'Bettor 2 richer': (100 x 0.8 + 300 x 0.4) / 400 = 0.50. Demo.tsx pool(). | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): (w p1 + w p2)/2w = (p1+p2)/2; preset 'Bettor 2 richer' with start beliefs: (100*0.8 + 300*0.4)/400 = 0.50. Presets keep the current beliefs, so the reveal's 'bettor 2's 40%' assumes the learner left beliefs at the start (non-blocking).

claims.text: When every bettor splits all their money by belief, the implied chance is the wealth-weighted average belief: each opinion counts in proportion to the money behind it.
claims.source: Money on A = sum of w_i p_i; pool = sum of w_i; ratio = sum (w_i / W) p_i. Demo.tsx pool(). | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): algebra: sum w_i p_i / sum w_i; pool() computes exactly this.

claims.text: Splitting all your money by belief is how a bettor who maximises the logarithm of their wealth bets in a pari-mutuel market.
claims.source: Easley and Kleinberg 2010, ch. 22; Kelly 1956 (Bell System Technical Journal 35). Fact-checker to confirm. | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): re-derived: maximise sum_i p_i log(b_i W o_i) subject to sum b_i = 1 gives b_i = p_i, independent of the odds, so it holds in a pari-mutuel pool with no take. Kelly, BSTJ 35(4):917-926 (1956) confirmed bibliographically via search; paper host blocked, not opened. Search found lecture notes on E&K 22.2 (horse races, betting, beliefs) stating the log-utility bettor bets fraction a_n and that odds are the wealth-weighted belief; E&K ch. 22 placement matches my knowledge (confident).

claims.text: The lesson is a simplified model: two bettors, no house cut, everyone bets all their money by belief.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Model: no house cut; all money bet by belief' and the reveal's last line. | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Demo.tsx: two bettors, no house cut, all money bet by belief; chip and muted line say so.

recall.question: Ana ($100) thinks a team wins 90%; Ben ($300) thinks 50%. Each bets all their money in proportion to belief. What chance do the odds imply?
recall.why: $90 + $150 = $240 of the $400 pool is on the team: 60%. Ben's belief counts three times as much because he has three times the money.
